new_note: *And they dealt treacherously with him, and formed a plot against him to slay him, but changing their minds, they sold him to Ishmaelite merchants, and they brought him down into Egypt, and they sold him to Potiphar, the eunuch of Pharaoh, the chief of the cooks, priest of the city of ’Êlêw. And the sons of Jacob slaughtered a kid, and dipped the coat of Joseph in the blood, and sent (it) to Jacob their father on the tenth of the seventh month.* (Jubilees 34:11–12). *And they hastened and took Joseph’s coat and tore it, and they killed a kid of the goats and dipped the coat in the blood of the kid, and then trampled it in the dust, and they sent the coat to their father Jacob by the hand of Naphtali, and they commanded him to say these words:* (Jasher 43:13). Jubilees folds the whole betrayal into two breaths: the plot to kill him, the change of heart, the sale to the Ishmaelites, the house of Potiphar, and then the kid slaughtered and the coat dipped in its blood and sent to Jacob. Jasher opens that second moment wider, the coat torn, the blood of the kid, the coat trampled in the dust and carried to their father by the hand of Naphtali with words the brothers put in his mouth. Both witnesses agree on the order: the sale came first, and the blood on the coat was a lie told afterward to cover it. Jubilees even dates the lie, the tenth of the seventh month, and goes on to say that this is why Yashar'el (Israel) afflicts itself on that day each year; the day a kid's blood was sent to deceive a father became the day of atonement.
member_note: Jubilees 34:11 — *they dealt treacherously with him, and formed a plot against him to slay him.* The sale that the bloodied coat of Jasher 43:13 was sent to hide.
flag: Card quotes 34:11–12 together; 34:12 (the kid and the dipped coat) is the verse that actually matches Jasher 43:13, and the old note quoted both.

new_note: *And the Egyptian saw the garment of Joseph and the broken door, and heard the words of his wife, and cast Joseph into prison into the place where the prisoners were kept whom the king imprisoned. And he was there in the prison; and Yahuah (God) gave Joseph favour in the sight of the chief of the prison guards and compassion before him, for he saw that Yahuah (God) was with him, and that Yahuah (God) made all that he did to prosper.* (Jubilees 39:11–12). *And Potiphar heard their words, and he placed him in the prison house, the place where the king’s prisoners are confined, and Joseph was in the house of confinement twelve years.* (Jasher 44:76). Both witnesses put Joseph in the same place, not a common jail but the prison where the king's own prisoners were kept, and Jasher adds that he was there twelve years. Jubilees adds what Jasher's one line does not, that Yahuah (God) was with him inside the prison, giving him favour with the chief of the guards and prospering everything he did. A master's anger chose the place, yet it was the one prison where Pharaoh's butler and baker would be sent, the only prison from which a road ran to the throne. Twelve years is a long time to be favoured in a cell, but the favour inside the walls was the same favour that would open them.
member_note: Jubilees 39:11 — *cast Joseph into prison into the place where the prisoners were kept whom the king imprisoned.* The king's own prison, where Jasher 44:76 keeps him twelve years and where the road to Pharaoh began.
flag: Card quotes 39:11–12 together, as the old note did; 39:12 carries the favour in prison that the old note's point rested on.

new_note: *But he did not surrender his soul, and he remembered Yahuah (God) and the words which Jacob, his father, used to read from amongst the words of Abraham, that no man should commit fornication with a woman who has a husband; that for him the punishment of death has been ordained in the heavens before the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God), and the sin will be recorded against him in the eternal books continually before Yahuah (God). And Joseph remembered these words and refused to lie with her.* (Jubilees 39:6–7). *And Joseph answered her, saying, It is better for me to remain in this house than to hearken to your words, to sin against Elohim; and she said to him, If you will not perform my wish, I will pluck out your eyes, add fetters to your feet, and will deliver you into the hands of them whom you did not know before.* (Jasher 44:78). Joseph's refusal did not come out of nowhere. Jubilees says he remembered the words of Abraham that his father Jacob used to read aloud, that a man who takes another man's wife has a death sentence written against him in heaven and a sin recorded in the eternal books, and because he remembered he refused. Jasher gives the same refusal in Joseph's own mouth, that he would rather stay in the house than sin against Elohim (God), and it cost him the threat of his eyes and fetters. Adultery was sin in Egypt long before there was a mountain called Sinai, because the commandment was older than the stone it was later written on. Joseph kept Torah because his fathers had kept it and read it to him.
member_note: Jubilees 39:6 — *he remembered Yahuah (God) and the words which Jacob, his father, used to read from amongst the words of Abraham.* The commandment Joseph kept in Jasher 44:78 was read aloud in his father's house before Sinai wrote it on stone.
flag: Card quotes 39:6–7 together, as the old note did; 39:7 is the refusal itself.

new_note: *And he set Joseph over all his house, and the blessing of Yahuah (God) came upon the house of the Egyptian on account of Joseph, and Yahuah (God) prospered him in all that he did.* (Jubilees 39:3). *And Potiphar took Joseph and brought him to his house that he might serve him, and Joseph found favor in the sight of Potiphar, and he placed confidence in him, and made him overseer over his house, and all that belonged to him he delivered over into his hand.* (Jasher 44:11). Jasher tells how Joseph came into Potiphar's house and found favour there until he was made overseer and everything was put in his hand. Jubilees tells what that meant for the house: the blessing of Yahuah (God) came upon the Egyptian's household on Joseph's account, and everything Potiphar did prospered. A slave sold out of Canaan carried the blessing of Abraham's house into a stranger's house, which is the promise to Abraham working in miniature, that in his seed the families of the earth would be blessed. Potiphar was blessed for the sake of the man he owned.
member_note: Jubilees 39:3 — *the blessing of Yahuah (God) came upon the house of the Egyptian on account of Joseph.* The overseer of Jasher 44:11 brought the blessing of Abraham's house into a stranger's house.

new_note: *And Yahudah (Judah) acknowledged, and said: “Tamar is more righteous than I am. And therefore let them burn her not.”* (Jubilees 41:19). *And Tamar rose up and put off the garments of her widowhood, and she put a vail upon her, and she entirely covered herself, and she went and sat in the public thoroughfare, which is upon the road to Timnah.* (Jasher 45:31). These two verses are the beginning and the end of one story. Jasher shows Tamar putting off her widow's garments, veiling herself and sitting on the road to Timnah; Jubilees shows Yahudah (Judah) at the end of it, confessing that she is more righteous than he and refusing to let her be burned. She was not on that road for harlotry. The seed of her dead husband's house was owed to her, Yahudah (Judah) had withheld Shelah, and she went and claimed what Torah gave her by the only door left open. When he saw the pledge he owned it, and the line that runs to Messiah (Christ) passes through the son she bore him.
member_note: Jubilees 41:19 — *Tamar is more righteous than I am. And therefore let them burn her not.* Yahudah's (Judah's) confession at the end of the road Tamar sat down on in Jasher 45:31.

new_note: *And Onan knew that the seed would not be his, (but) his brother’s only, and he went into the house of his brother’s wife, and spilt the seed on the ground, and he was wicked in the eyes of Yahuah (God), and He slew him.* (Jubilees 41:5). *And Onan took Tamar for a wife and he came to her, and Onan also did like to the work of his brother, and his work was evil in the sight of Yahuah (the Lord), and he slew him also.* (Jasher 45:26). Both witnesses say the same thing in almost the same words: Onan's work was evil in the eyes of Yahuah (God), and He slew him. Jubilees tells why it was evil. Onan knew the seed would not be counted his but his dead brother's, and he spilled it on the ground rather than raise a name for his brother. Jasher adds only that he did as his brother had done, which is to say the house of Yahudah (Judah) lost two sons to the same refusal. The judgment did not fall on lust; it fell on a man who took his brother's wife and would not give his brother a seed.
member_note: Jubilees 41:5 — *Onan knew that the seed would not be his, (but) his brother’s only.* Why the work of Jasher 45:26 was evil: he would not raise a seed for his dead brother.

new_note: *And he said before Pharaoh that his two dreams were one, and he said to him: “Seven years will come (in which there will be) plenty over all the land of Egypt, and after that seven years of famine, such a famine as has not been in all the land.* (Jubilees 40:3). *Behold the seven years that are coming there will be a great plenty throughout the land, and after that the seven years of famine will follow them, a very grievous famine; and all the plenty will be forgotten from the land, and the famine will consume the inhabitants of the land.* (Jasher 48:55). Joseph gave Pharaoh one reading for two dreams, and both witnesses carry the same reading word for word: seven years of plenty over the land, and after them seven years of famine such as had never been. Jasher's telling adds what the famine would do, that all the plenty would be forgotten and the famine would eat the inhabitants of the land. Jubilees says the two dreams were one, which is why the king needed a Hebrew and not a magician; the doubling was not two messages but one message fixed. The plenty was given so that the famine could be survived, and only one man in Egypt could see that.
member_note: Jubilees 40:3 — *he said before Pharaoh that his two dreams were one.* The same seven and seven that Jasher 48:55 unfolds, one reading for two dreams.

new_note: *And Yahuah (God) gave Joseph favour and mercy in the eyes of Pharaoh, and Pharaoh said to his servants: “We shall not find such a wise and discreet man as this man, for the spirit of Yahuah (God) is with him.”* (Jubilees 40:5). *And Joseph was then clothed with the spirit of Elohim before the king, and he knew all the things that would befall the king from that day forward, and he knew the proper interpretation of the king’s dream, and he spoke before the king.* (Jasher 48:52). Jasher shows the inside of the thing, Joseph clothed with the spirit of Elohim (God) before the king and knowing what would befall him from that day forward. Jubilees shows the outside, Pharaoh turning to his servants and saying out loud that the spirit of Yahuah (God) was with this man. A heathen king confessed what the court magicians could not produce. The wisdom was not Joseph's own, and Pharaoh knew it, which is why he did not look for a wiser Egyptian; there was none to find.
member_note: Jubilees 40:5 — *for the spirit of Yahuah (God) is with him.* Pharaoh's confession of the Spirit that Jasher 48:52 says clothed Joseph before the king.

new_note: *And then the chief butler remembered Joseph and spake of him to the king, and he brought him forth from the prison, and he told his two dreams before him.* (Jubilees 40:2). *And there was with us a Hebrew servant belonging to the captain of the guard, his name was Joseph, for his master had been angry with him and placed him in the house of confinement, and he attended us there.* (Jasher 48:33). Jubilees gives the hinge in one verse, the chief butler remembering Joseph and speaking of him to the king, and Joseph brought up out of the prison. Jasher gives the butler's actual words, a Hebrew servant of the captain of the guard, put in the house of confinement by an angry master, who attended us there. The man who brought Joseph before Pharaoh was a man Joseph had served in a cell. The service he gave in confinement was the road that carried him out of it, and the one who had forgotten him was the one Yahuah (God) used to remember him.
member_note: Jubilees 40:2 — *the chief butler remembered Joseph and spake of him to the king.* The remembrance that Jasher 48:33 puts into the butler's own words before Pharaoh.

new_note: *And in those days Pharaoh dreamed two dreams in one night concerning a famine which was to be in all the land, and he awoke from his sleep and called all the interpreters of dreams that were in Egypt, and magicians, and told them his two dreams, and they were not able to declare (them).* (Jubilees 40:1). *At that time Pharaoh king of Egypt was sitting upon his throne in the land of Egypt, and lay in his bed and dreamed dreams, and Pharaoh saw in his dream that he was standing by the side of the river of Egypt.* (Jasher 48:2). Jasher sets the scene, Pharaoh on his bed in the land of Egypt, dreaming that he stood by the river. Jubilees tells what the dreams were about and what came of them: two dreams in one night concerning a famine, and all the interpreters and magicians of Egypt called in and unable to say what they meant. Yahuah (God) spoke to a heathen king in his sleep and shut the meaning from every wise man in his court, so that the only door left open was a Hebrew slave in the king's prison. The famine was coming either way; the dream was mercy, and the silence of the magicians was the thing that got Joseph out.
member_note: Jubilees 40:1 — *Pharaoh dreamed two dreams in one night concerning a famine which was to be in all the land.* The dreams Jasher 48:2 begins at the river, and the magicians who could not read them.

new_note: *And Joseph ruled over all the land of Egypt, and all the princes of Pharaoh, and all his servants, and all who did the king’s business loved him, for he walked in uprightness, for he was without pride and arrogance, and he had no respect of persons, and did not accept gifts, but he judged in uprightness all the people of the land.* (Jubilees 40:8). *And at the revolution of the year, in the second year of Joseph’s reigning over Egypt, Yahuah (the Lord) gave great plenty throughout the land for seven years as Joseph had spoken, for Yahuah (the Lord) blessed all the produce of the earth in those days for seven years, and they ate and were greatly satisfied.* (Jasher 50:7). Jasher tells of the second year of Joseph's reign, when Yahuah (the Lord) gave the great plenty for seven years exactly as Joseph had spoken. Jubilees tells what kind of man was reigning while the plenty came: one who walked in uprightness, without pride, with no respect of persons, who took no gifts and judged all the people of the land fairly. That is the judge Torah later requires of Yashar'el (Israel), and here he is, a Hebrew ruling Egypt. The land was fed under a ruler who could not be bought, and the princes and servants loved him for it.
member_note: Jubilees 40:8 — *he had no respect of persons, and did not accept gifts, but he judged in uprightness.* The ruler under whom the seven years of plenty in Jasher 50:7 came to the land.

new_note: *(Now the famine was very sore in the land of Canaan), and Jacob heard that there was food in Egypt, and he sent his ten sons that they should procure food for him in Egypt; but Benjamin he did not send, and (the ten sons of Jacob) arrived (in Egypt) among those that went (there.)* (Jubilees 42:4). *And Jacob afterward heard that there was corn in Egypt, and he called to his sons to go to Egypt to buy corn, for upon them also did the famine prevail, and he called to his sons, saying,* (Jasher 51:1). Both witnesses put the same scene at the door of the reunion: Jacob hearing that there is food in Egypt and sending his sons down to buy it, because the famine had reached Canaan too. Jubilees adds the detail the whole testing turns on, that he sent ten and kept Benjamin home. The famine that drove the ten down was the same famine Joseph had been set over, so the sons of Jacob were walking toward the brother they had sold without knowing it. Benjamin being withheld is what gave Joseph the lever he would use to find out whether they had changed.
member_note: Jubilees 42:4 — *he sent his ten sons that they should procure food for him in Egypt; but Benjamin he did not send.* The descent of the ten that Jasher 51:1 opens, with Benjamin kept at home.

new_note: *And Joseph saw that they were all accordant in goodness one with another, and he could not refrain himself, and he told them that he was Joseph.* (Jubilees 43:14). *And Joseph observed all their acts, and said to them, Why do you look here and there? I am Joseph whom you sold to Egypt, now therefore let it not grieve you that you sold me, for as a support during the famine did Elohim send me before you.* (Jasher 54:69). Jubilees tells exactly when Joseph broke: when he saw that his brothers were all of one accord in goodness toward one another, he could not hold himself and told them who he was. Jasher gives the words, I am Joseph whom you sold to Egypt, and the comfort that came with them, that Elohim (God) had sent him ahead of them to keep them alive through the famine. He did not reveal himself to the men who had sold him; he waited until he saw them stand together for Benjamin, which was the opposite of what they had done to him. The test was whether they had changed, and when they had, the hidden brother showed his face.
member_note: Jubilees 43:14 — *Joseph saw that they were all accordant in goodness one with another, and he could not refrain himself.* The moment Joseph could hold back no longer, and the words he said in Jasher 54:69.

new_note: *Now rather let me, your servant, abide instead of the boy as a bondsman to my lord, and let the lad go with his brethren, for I became surety for him at the hand of your servant our father, and if I do not bring him back, your servant will bear the blame to our father for ever."* (Jubilees 43:13). *And Judah answered Joseph, saying, Surely you must know that I was security for the lad to his father, saying, If I brought him not to him I should bear his blame forever.* (Jasher 54:57). Jasher and Jubilees carry Yahudah's (Judah's) plea almost word for word: he had become surety for the lad to his father, and if he did not bring him back he would bear the blame for ever. Jubilees adds the offer that goes with it, let me stay as a bondsman in the boy's place and let the lad go home with his brothers. The brother who once proposed selling Joseph now offers himself as a slave so that Rachel's other son can go free. That is the change Joseph was waiting to see, and it is why the next thing in the story is Joseph weeping and telling them who he is.
member_note: Jubilees 43:13 — *let me, your servant, abide instead of the boy as a bondsman to my lord.* The surety plea of Jasher 54:57, with Yahudah (Judah) offering himself in Benjamin's place.

new_note: *And Bâlâq, the son of Beor, reigned in Edom, and the name of his city was Danâbâ.* (Jubilees 38:16). *And all the children of Esau took him and anointed him and they crowned him for a king, and they bowed down to him, and they said to him, May the king live, may the king live.* (Jasher 57:42). Jubilees gives the name and the city, Balaq the son of Beor reigning in Edom from Danaba. Jasher shows the crowning itself, the children of Esau anointing a king and bowing to him and shouting that the king should live. Edom had a throne and a shout of loyalty while the sons of Jacob were still a family of shepherds, and long before Yashar'el (Israel) asked for a king of its own. The elder brother built a kingdom first; it did not make him the heir.
member_note: Jubilees 38:16 — *Bâlâq, the son of Beor, reigned in Edom, and the name of his city was Danâbâ.* The first king of Edom, whose crowning Jasher 57:42 shows with the shout, May the king live.
flag: Jasher 57:42 as supplied does not name Bela/Balaq or his city; the name must sit in a nearby verse. The note treats 57:42 as the crowning scene only.

new_note: *And the sons of Jacob pressed hard upon the sons of Esau in the mountains of Seir, and bowed their necks so that they became servants of the sons of Jacob.* (Jubilees 38:10). *And it came to pass after the battle, the children of Esau turned back and came home to Seir, and the children of Esau slew those who had remained in the land of the children of Seir; they slew also their wives and little ones, they left not a soul alive except fifty young lads and damsels whom they suffered to live, and the children of Esau did not put them to death, and the lads became their slaves, and the damsels they took for wives.* (Jasher 57:35). These are two layers of the same mountain. Jubilees shows the sons of Jacob pressing the sons of Esau hard in Seir and bowing their necks until they served Jacob's sons. Jasher shows what the sons of Esau did when they came home from battle to Seir: they slaughtered the Horites who were left, wives and little ones, and kept only fifty lads and damsels, the lads as slaves and the damsels as wives. The ones made servants of Jacob turned and made servants of others, and the land of Seir changed hands by the sword twice over. Esau's house was always strong against the weak and bowed before the brother it hated.
member_note: Jubilees 38:10 — *the sons of Jacob pressed hard upon the sons of Esau in the mountains of Seir, and bowed their necks.* Esau's sons bowed under Jacob's sons, and in Jasher 57:35 bowing the Horites under themselves.
flag: Different events: Jubilees 38:10 is Jacob's sons subduing Esau's sons; Jasher 57:35 is Esau's sons slaughtering and enslaving the Horites of Seir. The link is the mountain of Seir and the pattern, not one battle.

new_note: *And Simeon and Benjamin and Enoch, Reuben’s son, went forth on the west side of the tower, and fifty (men) with them, and they slew of Edom and of the Horites four hundred men, stout warriors; and six hundred fled, and four of the sons of Esau fled with them, and left their father lying slain, as he had fallen on the hill which is in ’Adûrâm.* (Jubilees 38:8). *And the battle was heavy between them, and the sons of Esau were smitten before the sons of Jacob, and the sons of Jacob slew of the sons of Esau eighty men, and not one died of the people of the sons of Jacob; and the hand of Joseph prevailed over all the people of the sons of Esau, and he took Zepho, the son of Eliphaz, the son of Esau, and fifty of his men captive, and he bound them with chains of iron, and gave them into the hand of his servants to bring them to Egypt.* (Jasher 57:2). Both witnesses tell of the sons of Jacob prevailing over the sons of Esau in the country of Seir, but they are not the same battle. Jubilees tells the one in which Esau himself fell on the hill at Aduram, Simeon and Benjamin and Reuben's son Enoch going out from the west side of the tower and slaying four hundred of Edom and the Horites. Jasher tells the later war, when Joseph's hand prevailed, eighty of Esau's sons fell and not one of Jacob's, and Zepho was taken in iron chains to Egypt. The feud did not end with Esau's death; his grandchildren came back for more and were beaten again. The enmity between the two brothers' houses outlived both brothers.
member_note: Jubilees 38:8 — *they slew of Edom and of the Horites four hundred men, stout warriors.* The war in which Esau fell; Jasher 57:2 is the later one where Joseph took Zepho in chains.
flag: Different battles: Jubilees 38:8 is the war in Jacob's lifetime where Esau is slain (400 killed); Jasher 57:2 is the war after Jacob's death where Joseph prevails and Zepho is captured (80 killed). The note says so plainly rather than calling them the same battle.

new_note: *And it came to pass that after Jacob died the children of Yashar’el (Israel) multiplied in the land of Egypt, and they became a great nation, and they were of one accord in heart, so that brother loved brother and every man helped his brother, and they increased abundantly and multiplied exceedingly, ten weeks of years, all the days of the life of Joseph.* (Jubilees 46:1). *In that year, being the seventy-ninth year of the Israelites going down to Egypt, died Reuben the son of Jacob, in the land of Egypt; Reuben was a hundred and twenty-five years old when he died, and they put him into a coffin, and he was given into the hands of his children.* (Jasher 62:1). Jasher counts this season by funerals, and here it is Reuben, dead at a hundred and twenty-five in the seventy-ninth year of the going down, put into a coffin and left in his children's keeping. Jubilees counts the same season by the living: after Jacob died the children of Yashar'el (Israel) multiplied in Egypt and became a great nation, brother loving brother, for ten weeks of years, all the days of Joseph. The fathers were being laid in coffins one by one while the seed grew into a people in a land that was not theirs. Both things were happening at once, and both had been told to Abram beforehand.
member_note: Jubilees 46:1 — *they became a great nation, and they were of one accord in heart, so that brother loved brother.* The multiplying that Jasher 62:1 counts by the deaths of the fathers, Reuben first.

new_note: *And Joseph died in the forty-sixth jubilee, in the sixth week, in the second year, and they buried him in the land of Egypt, and his brethren died after him.* (Jubilees 46:8). *And it came to pass at that time that Judah the son of Jacob died in Egypt, in the eighty-sixth year of Jacob’s going down to Egypt, and Judah was a hundred and twenty-nine years old at his death, and they embalmed him and put him into a coffin, and he was given into the hands of his children.* (Jasher 62:23). Jubilees says it in one breath: Joseph died and was buried in Egypt, and his brethren died after him. Jasher spreads that one breath across a roll of dated deaths, and this entry is Yahudah (Judah), a hundred and twenty-nine years old in the eighty-sixth year of the going down, embalmed and put into a coffin and given to his children. The embalming and the coffin were not Egyptian vanity. The fathers were being kept, not buried, because the family knew they were going home and the bones were going with them.
member_note: Jubilees 46:8 — *they buried him in the land of Egypt, and his brethren died after him.* The brethren dying after Joseph, counted one by one in Jasher 62; here Yahudah (Judah) at 129.

new_note: *And Joseph died in the forty-sixth jubilee, in the sixth week, in the second year, and they buried him in the land of Egypt, and his brethren died after him.* (Jubilees 46:8). *For Zepho heard that the mighty men of Egypt were dead and that Joseph and his brethren the sons at Jacob were dead, and that all their children the children of Israel remained in Egypt.* (Jasher 64:8). The death of Joseph and his brethren was not only a grief inside Yashar'el (Israel); it was a signal outside it. Jasher shows Zepho, Esau's grandson, hearing that the mighty men of Egypt were dead and that Joseph and his brethren were dead, and that only their children remained, and that is when he moved. Jubilees gives the deaths plainly, Joseph in the forty-sixth jubilee and his brethren after him. Enemies wait for the generation of the fathers to pass before they come against the children, and the king who knew not Joseph was of the same mind as Zepho.
member_note: Jubilees 46:8 — *Joseph died in the forty-sixth jubilee, in the sixth week, in the second year.* The death that Zepho was waiting for in Jasher 64:8 before he came against the children.

new_note: *And they made them serve with rigour, and the more they dealt evilly with them, the more they increased and multiplied.* (Jubilees 46:15). *And when they ploughed they were unable to hurt the infants of the children of Israel, so the people increased and waxed exceedingly.* (Jasher 67:59). Jubilees gives the rule: the more Egypt dealt evilly with them, the more they increased and multiplied. Jasher gives the strangest proof of it, the Egyptians ploughing the ground where the Hebrew women had given birth and finding they could not harm the infants, so the people grew all the more. Rigour, ploughing, and later the river, and every one of them a failure. What was meant to cut off the seed became the thing under which it multiplied, because the one who had promised Abraham a seed like the sand of the sea was the one keeping count.
member_note: Jubilees 46:15 — *the more they dealt evilly with them, the more they increased and multiplied.* The rule Jasher 67:59 proves with ploughs that could not hurt the infants.

new_note: *And Pharaoh, king of Egypt, issued a command regarding them that they should cast all their male children which were born into the river.* (Jubilees 47:2). *If it please the king let him order all their children which shall be born from this day forward, to be thrown into the water, for by this can you wipe away their name, for none of them, nor of their fathers, were tried in this manner.* (Jasher 67:49). Jubilees gives the decree, Pharaoh commanding that every male child born to them be thrown into the river. Jasher gives where the decree came from: Balaam counselling the king to throw the children into the water, and saying the aim out loud, by this you can wipe away their name. The war was never only about numbers; it was against the name of the seed. The same Balaam would later be hired to curse that seed in the wilderness, and here he is already at work before Moses was born. The order came from a prophet for hire before it came from a king.
member_note: Jubilees 47:2 — *they should cast all their male children which were born into the river.* The decree Balaam counselled in Jasher 67:49 to wipe away their name.

new_note: *And in those days Tharmuth, the daughter of Pharaoh, came to bathe in the river, and she heard your voice crying, and she told her maidens to bring you forth, and they brought you to her.* (Jubilees 47:5). *And Bathia lifted up her eyes to the river, and she saw the ark upon the water, and sent her maid to fetch it.* (Jasher 68:18). Jubilees calls her Tharmuth and Jasher calls her Bathia, but both set the same scene: Pharaoh's daughter at the river, seeing or hearing the child, and sending her maid to bring it up out of the water. The river was the decree; the rescue came out of the very river, and by the hand of Pharaoh's own house. Jubilees tells it to Moses in the second person, she heard your voice crying, because this is the Angel reciting Moses' own life back to him. The king's daughter undid the king's command without knowing it.
member_note: Jubilees 47:5 — *Tharmuth, the daughter of Pharaoh, came to bathe in the river, and she heard your voice crying.* Pharaoh's daughter at the river, named Bathia in Jasher 68:18, lifting the child out of the decree.

new_note: *And Pharaoh, king of Egypt, issued a command regarding them that they should cast all their male children which were born into the river.* (Jubilees 47:2). *And Pharaoh sent his officers to take the children and slay them; thus did the Egyptians to the Hebrew women all the days.* (Jasher 68:11). Jubilees gives the decree; Jasher shows it in force, Pharaoh's officers sent out to take the children and slay them, and the note that this was done to the Hebrew women all the days. The command was not a single bad night. It was a standing order carried out every day, and that is the Egypt Moses was born into. His mother's ark on the water was an answer to a decree that had been running for years, and it had to be hidden because the officers were still coming.
member_note: Jubilees 47:2 — *Pharaoh, king of Egypt, issued a command regarding them.* The decree that Jasher 68:11 shows carried out by Pharaoh's officers all the days.

new_note: *And afterwards, when you were grown up, they brought you to the daughter of Pharaoh, and you did become her son, and Amram your father taught you writing, and after you had completed three weeks they brought you into the royal court.* (Jubilees 47:9). *And when Moses grew up in the king’s house, Bathia the daughter of Pharaoh considered him as a son, and all the household of Pharaoh honored him, and all the men of Egypt were afraid of him.* (Jasher 70:33). Jasher tells it from the outside: Moses grown in the king's house, Bathia counting him as her son, the household honouring him and all Egypt afraid of him. Jubilees tells it to Moses himself, the Angel reciting his own life back to him in the second person, you became her son, and they brought you into the royal court. But Jubilees keeps one thing Jasher does not: before the court had him, Amram his father taught him writing. The Hebrew father's teaching came first, and then Pharaoh's house. He was raised in the court, but he was taught at home.
member_note: Jubilees 47:9 — *Amram your father taught you writing, and after you had completed three weeks they brought you into the royal court.* The son of Pharaoh's daughter in Jasher 70:33, who was taught by Amram before the court had him.

new_note: *And you were three weeks of years at court until the time when you did go forth from the royal court and did see an Egyptian smiting your friend who was of the children of Yashar’el (Israel), and you did slay him and hide him in the sand.* (Jubilees 47:10). *At that time that the war and the siege were against Cush, Moses fled from Egypt from Pharaoh who sought to kill him for having slain the Egyptian.* (Jasher 72:21). Jubilees gives the deed, told to Moses as his own memory: he went out from the court, saw an Egyptian smiting his friend of the children of Yashar'el (Israel), slew him and hid him in the sand. Jasher gives what followed, Moses fleeing because Pharaoh sought to kill him for it, and sets the flight in the days of the war against Cush. The man raised in the king's house chose the beaten Hebrew over the court that raised him, and it cost him the court. Three weeks of years in Pharaoh's palace ended in a day over one afflicted brother.
member_note: Jubilees 47:10 — *did see an Egyptian smiting your friend who was of the children of Yashar’el (Israel), and you did slay him.* The slaying that sent Moses out of Egypt in Jasher 72:21.

new_note: *And it came to pass, when the sun had set, that an ecstasy fell upon Abram, and lo! an horror of great darkness fell upon him, and it was said to Abram: “Know of a surety that your seed shall be a stranger in a land (that is) not theirs, and they will bring them into bondage, and afflict them four hundred years.* (Jubilees 14:13). *For they said the period was completed which Yahuah (the Lord) had appointed to the children of Israel in the times of old, which he had spoken to Abraham.* (Jasher 75:2). Jubilees gives the word to Abram in the darkness: his seed would be strangers in a land not theirs, brought into bondage and afflicted four hundred years. Jasher shows what happened when that word was reckoned wrongly. The children of Ephraim said the period Yahuah (the Lord) had appointed was complete, and went out of Egypt before the time, and the chapter that follows tells of their slaughter. A true word misreckoned kills as surely as a false one. The years were fixed, but they were Yahuah's (God's) to count, and the ones who counted for Him died at the hands of the Philistines.
member_note: Jubilees 14:13 — *your seed shall be a stranger in a land (that is) not theirs, and they will bring them into bondage.* The appointed years that the sons of Ephraim in Jasher 75:2 counted finished before they were.

new_note: *And in the sixth year of the third week of the forty-ninth jubilee you did depart and dwell in the land of Midian five weeks and one year. And you did return into Egypt in the second week in the second year in the fiftieth jubilee.* (Jubilees 48:1). *So Moses went to Midian, for he was afraid to return to Egypt on account of Pharaoh, and he went and sat at a well of water in Midian.* (Jasher 76:13). Jasher gives the first scene of the Midian years, Moses afraid to go back to Egypt, sitting down at a well. Jubilees gives their length, five weeks of years and one year, and the date he went in and the date he came out, down to the week and the jubilee. The one who would stand before Pharaoh spent the better part of his life first as a fugitive at a well. The years are counted so carefully because none of them were wasted; the man who returned in the fiftieth jubilee was not the man who fled in the forty-ninth.
member_note: Jubilees 48:1 — *you did depart and dwell in the land of Midian five weeks and one year.* The length of the sojourn that Jasher 76:13 begins at a well.

new_note: *And everything took place according to your words; ten great and terrible judgments came on the land of Egypt that you might execute vengeance on it for Yashar’el (Israel). And Yahuah (God) did everything for Yashar’el’s (Israel’s) sake, and according to His covenant, which He had ordained with Abraham that He would take vengeance on them as they had brought them by force into bondage.* (Jubilees 48:7–8). *And Yahuah (the Lord) heard the cries of the children of Israel, and saw the oppression with which the Egyptians oppressed them.* (Jasher 78:15). Jasher gives the hearing and the seeing: Yahuah (the Lord) heard the cries of the children of Yashar'el (Israel) and saw the oppression. Jubilees gives what came of it, ten great and terrible judgments on Egypt, and says plainly what they were for, vengeance for Yashar'el (Israel) according to the covenant Yahuah (God) had ordained with Abraham. The plagues were not random wrath against a nation; they were a Father keeping an oath sworn four hundred years earlier, that the nation which brought Abraham's seed into bondage by force would be judged for it. He heard, He saw, and then He struck, and every one of the ten came according to the word of Moses.
member_note: Jubilees 48:7 — *ten great and terrible judgments came on the land of Egypt that you might execute vengeance on it.* The answer to the cries Yahuah (the Lord) heard in Jasher 78:15.
flag: Card quotes 48:7–8 together, as the old note did; 48:8 carries the covenant with Abraham that the old note's point rested on.

new_note: *And in the sixth year of the third week of the forty-ninth jubilee you did depart and dwell in the land of Midian five weeks and one year. And you did return into Egypt in the second week in the second year in the fiftieth jubilee.* (Jubilees 48:1). *In those days Moses, the son of Amram, in Midian, took Zipporah, the daughter of Reuel the Midianite, for a wife.* (Jasher 78:7). Jubilees gives the Midian years in a date, from the forty-ninth jubilee to the fiftieth, five weeks of years and one year. Jasher puts a marriage inside those years, Moses taking Zipporah the daughter of Reuel the Midianite for a wife. The deliverer of Yashar'el (Israel) married outside the camp and kept sheep for a stranger before he ever lifted a rod, and the years are not written as a gap in his story. They are dated to the week because Yahuah (God) was counting them as the preparation of the man.
member_note: Jubilees 48:1 — *you did return into Egypt in the second week in the second year in the fiftieth jubilee.* The dated sojourn in which Jasher 78:7 places the marriage to Zipporah.

new_note: *And we did not lead forth the children of Yashar’el (Israel) from Egypt empty handed.* (Jubilees 48:19). *And at the end of two hundred and ten years, Yahuah (the Lord) brought forth the children of Israel from Egypt with a strong hand.* (Jasher 81:4). The we of Jubilees is the Angel of the Presence speaking, telling Moses that they did not bring the children of Yashar'el (Israel) out of Egypt empty handed. Jasher gives the same going out in its sum, two hundred and ten years ended and Yahuah (the Lord) bringing them out with a strong hand. Angels led and the strong hand of Yahuah (the Lord) drove, and the people walked out carrying the wages of their bondage. The bondage was real and the years were counted, and when the counting was done they left as a nation paid, not as slaves escaped.
member_note: Jubilees 48:19 — *we did not lead forth the children of Yashar’el (Israel) from Egypt empty handed.* The going out that Jasher 81:4 sums up with a strong hand after two hundred and ten years.

new_note: *And the king of Egypt went forth to war with the king of Canaan in the forty-seventh jubilee, in the second week in the second year, and the children of Yashar’el (Israel) brought forth all the bones of the children of Jacob save the bones of Joseph, and they buried them in the field in the double cave in the mountain.* (Jubilees 46:9). *And it was in those days, when the children of Israel were dwelling securely in their cities, that they buried the coffins of the tribes of their ancestors, which they had brought up from Egypt, each man in the inheritance of his children, the twelve sons of Jacob did the children of Israel bury, each man in the possession of his children.* (Jasher 90:38). Both witnesses agree the sons of Jacob did not stay in Egypt's ground; they differ on when their bones went home. Jubilees has them carried up early, while the king of Egypt was off at war with Canaan, and laid in the double cave in the mountain, all but Joseph. Jasher has the coffins carried up out of Egypt at the exodus and buried after the land had rest, each man in the inheritance of his own children. Either way the fathers were waiting for the land and were brought into it. Joseph alone, in Jubilees' telling, had to wait for the whole nation to come out with him.
member_note: Jubilees 46:9 — *brought forth all the bones of the children of Jacob save the bones of Joseph.* The bones of the brethren going home; Jasher 90:38 buries them later, each in his own inheritance.
flag: Jubilees 46:9 and Jasher 90:38 give different times and places for the burial (early, at the double cave in Hebron vs after the conquest, each in his tribal inheritance). The note states the difference rather than hiding it.

new_note: *For all the land which you see I shall give to you and to your seed for ever, and I shall make your seed as the sand of the sea: though a man may number the dust of the earth, yet your seed shall not be numbered.* (Jubilees 13:20). *And Yahuah (the Lord) gave to the children of Israel the whole land of Canaan, as he had sworn to their ancestors, and Yahuah (the Lord) gave them rest from those around them, and the children of Israel dwelt securely in their cities.* (Jasher 91:15). Jubilees gives the promise to Abram as he stood looking at the land: all of it to him and to his seed for ever, and a seed past counting. Jasher gives the receipt generations later, Yahuah (the Lord) giving the children of Yashar'el (Israel) the whole land of Canaan as he had sworn to their ancestors, and rest from those around them. The oath was to a man and his bloodline, and it was kept to the bloodline. The word in Jubilees is for ever, which means the land grant did not expire with Joshua or with any later exile; the same seed is still the heir.
member_note: Jubilees 13:20 — *all the land which you see I shall give to you and to your seed for ever.* The oath to Abram that Jasher 91:15 shows kept to his seed.

new_note: *And He made for them coats of skin, and clothed them, and sent them forth from the Garden of Eden.* (Jubilees 3:26). *And the cherub who guarded the garden was standing at the western gate, and guarding it against Adam and Eve, lest they should suddenly come into the garden. And the cherub turned around, as if to put them to death; according to the commandment Elohim (God) had given him.* (1 Adam and Eve 54:3). Jubilees gives the sending out in one verse: coats of skin, clothed, sent forth from the garden. The First Book of Adam and Eve shows what the sending out meant afterward, a cherub standing at the western gate, guarding it against the two of them and turning as if to kill them, because that was the commandment Elohim (God) had given him. They were clothed and shut out in the same hour. The coats were mercy and the sword at the gate was judgment, and both came by commandment from the same hand. There was no sneaking back into the garden; the way back would have to be opened from the inside.
member_note: Jubilees 3:26 — *He made for them coats of skin, and clothed them, and sent them forth from the Garden of Eden.* The expulsion that 1 Adam and Eve 54:3 guards with a cherub at the gate.
flag: Old note said a shut eastern gate; the supplied 1 Adam and Eve 54:3 text says the western gate. Note follows the text.

new_note: *And they will make to themselves high places and groves and graven images, and they will worship, each his own (graven image), so as to go astray, and they will sacrifice their children to demons, and to all the works of the error of their hearts.* (Jubilees 1:11). *And he ordained him priests for the high places, and for the devils, and for the calves which he had made.* (2 Chronicles 11:15). What Yahuah (God) told Moses on the mountain they would do, Jeroboam did in Bethel and Dan: high places, devils, and calves of his own making, with priests ordained to serve them. Jubilees calls the devils demons and adds the worst of it, children sacrificed to them. The golden calf was not a one-time fall at the foot of Sinai; it came back as a state religion with its own priesthood and its own altars. Going astray always builds a high place and ordains someone to tend it, and the error of the heart ends in the blood of the children.
member_note: Jubilees 1:11 — *they will make to themselves high places and groves and graven images.* The pattern foretold to Moses, which Jeroboam built and staffed in 2 Chronicles 11:15.
